The person's stated priority is that computational audits are paramount — if stated values are wrong, the totality of the mathematics is in jeopardy — while noting that the stale self-description and production/cosmetic classes are not a concern and will resolve before print. The person is anticipating the full audit taking approximately a week and expressed hope the prior rulings and known error patterns might accelerate it.

The session then executed the gate on BUILD94 and BUILD95 (both passing all checks), recorded all rulings in W-106, built a reusable clerical checker (r2-tools.py including a global constants check across all six volumes), and completed Phase R2 segments for main Chapters 7, 8, and 9 with per-chapter instruments (r2-ch7.py, r2-ch8.py, r2-ch9.py). Every tower-computable claim in Chapters 7 and 8 reproduced exactly. Chapter 9 yielded two subject-matter defects found only by testing on all lattice pairs rather than the printed sample: the μ_Λ = μ_arith biconditional is false in general (true only on unit hypercubes), and d's "form 1 counts cells" is false for 71.7% of pairs. The global constants check confirmed every printed tower value consistent across all six volumes with no off-by-one variants. The session closed with BUILD96 (2,922,763 B, md5 9dac8d6b…, 154 members) and HANDOFF-21 delivered.

**Tool Knowledge**

Google Drive searches using `title contains 'BUILD95' or title contains 'HANDOFF-20'` with `excludeContentSnippets=True` and `pageSize=10` are the reliable fetch pattern; the first attempt in this session returned nothing despite the files being present, and a second attempt after the person confirmed their presence succeeded. Both bundle files (main and compendia) must be fetched and decoded from their spill paths at `/mnt/user-data/tool_results/<tool_use_id>.json` using `base64.b64decode(json.loads(json.load(open(p))[0]['text'])['content'], validate=True)` — never hand-transcribed. The shell `/bin/sh` is dash; `printf` mangles `\x27` (a literal backslash-x27 appears instead of an apostrophe) — all text with apostrophes or non-ASCII must be written via Python. Every shell call requires `timeout 280`. Files must never be copied over existing files; always list the target directory first.

1	---
     2	name: file-reading
     3	description: "Use this skill when a file has been uploaded but its content is NOT in your context — only its path at /mnt/user-data/uploads/ is listed in an uploaded_files block. This skill is a router: it tells you which tool to use for each file type (pdf, docx, xlsx, csv, json, images, archives, ebooks) so you read the right amount the right way instead of blindly running cat on a binary. Triggers: any mention of /mnt/user-data/uploads/, an uploaded_files section, a file_path tag, or a user asking about an uploaded file you have not yet read. Do NOT use this skill if the file content is already visible in your context inside a documents block — you already have it."
     4	compatibility: "claude.ai, Claude Desktop, Cowork — any surface where uploads land at /mnt/user-data/uploads/"
     5	license: Proprietary. LICENSE.txt has complete terms
     6	---
     7	
     8	# Reading Uploaded Files
     9	
    10	## Why this skill exists
    11	
    12	When a user uploads a file in claude.ai, Claude Desktop, or Cowork,
    13	the file is written to `/mnt/user-data/uploads/<filename>` and you are told the path
    14	in an `<uploaded_files>` block. **The content is not in your context.**
    15	You must go read it.
    16	
    17	The naive thing — `cat /mnt/user-data/uploads/whatever` — is wrong for
    18	most files:
    19	
    20	- On a PDF it prints binary garbage.
    21	- On a 100MB CSV it floods your context with rows you will never use.
    22	- On a DOCX it prints the raw ZIP bytes.
    23	- On an image it does nothing useful at all.
    24	
    25	This skill tells you the right first move for each type, and when to
    26	hand off to a deeper skill.
    27	
    28	## General protocol
    29	
    30	1. **Look at the extension.** That is your dispatch key.
    31	2. **Stat before you read.** Large files need sampling, not slurping.
    32	   ```bash
    33	   stat -c '%s bytes, %y' /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    34	   file /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    35	   ```
    36	3. **Read just enough to answer the user's question.** If they asked
    37	   "how many rows are in this CSV", don't load the whole thing into
    38	   pandas — `wc -l` gives a fast approximation (it counts newlines,
    39	   not CSV records, so it may over-count if quoted fields contain
    40	   embedded newlines).
    41	4. **If a dedicated skill exists, go read it.** The table below tells
    42	   you when. The dedicated skills cover editing, creating, and advanced
    43	   operations that this skill does not.
    44	
    45	## `extract-text`
    46	
    47	For docx, odt, epub, xlsx, pptx, rtf, and ipynb the first move is
    48	`extract-text <file>`. It emits markdown for docx/odt/epub (headings,
    49	bold, lists, links, tables), tab-separated rows under `## Sheet:`
    50	headers for xlsx, text under `## Slide N` headers for pptx, fenced
    51	code cells for ipynb, and plain text for rtf. Pass `--format <fmt>`
    52	when the extension is wrong or absent (e.g., `--format xlsx` on an
    53	`.xlsm`). If it errors on a file, `pandoc <file> -t plain` is a
    54	fallback; for xlsx/pptx, fall back to the dedicated skill's
    55	Python-based approach (openpyxl / python-pptx).
    56	
    57	## Dispatch table
    58	
    59	Where a dedicated skill is named below, invoke it by name if you have a
    60	Skill tool, or Read its SKILL.md (listed in your available skills, or in
    61	the same skills directory as this file).
    62	
    63	| Extension                         | First move                                           | Dedicated skill |
    64	| --------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | --------------- |
    65	| `.pdf`                            | Content inventory (see PDF section)                  | `pdf-reading`   |
    66	| `.docx`                           | `extract-text`                                       | `docx`          |
    67	| `.doc` (legacy)                   | Convert to `.docx` first                             | `docx`          |
    68	| `.xlsx`                           | `extract-text`                                       | `xlsx`          |
    69	| `.xlsm`                           | `extract-text --format xlsx`                         | `xlsx`          |
    70	| `.xls` (legacy)                   | `pd.read_excel(engine="xlrd")` — openpyxl rejects it | `xlsx`          |
    71	| `.ods`                            | `pd.read_excel(engine="odf")` — openpyxl rejects it  | `xlsx`          |
    72	| `.pptx`                           | `extract-text`                                       | `pptx`          |
    73	| `.ppt` (legacy)                   | Convert to `.pptx` first                             | `pptx`          |
    74	| `.csv`, `.tsv`                    | `pandas` with `nrows`                                | — (below)       |
    75	| `.json`, `.jsonl`                 | `jq` for structure                                   | — (below)       |
    76	| `.jpg`, `.png`, `.gif`, `.webp`   | Already in your context as vision input              | — (below)       |
    77	| `.zip`, `.tar`, `.tar.gz`         | List contents, do **not** auto-extract               | — (below)       |
    78	| `.gz` (single file)               | `zcat \| head` — no manifest to list                 | — (below)       |
    79	| `.epub`, `.odt`                   | `extract-text`                                       | — (below)       |
    80	| `.rtf`                            | `extract-text`                                       | — (below)       |
    81	| `.ipynb`                          | `extract-text`                                       | — (below)       |
    82	| `.txt`, `.md`, `.log`, code files | `wc -c` then `head` or full `cat`                    | — (below)       |
    83	| Unknown                           | `file` then decide                                   | —               |
    84	
    85	---
    86	
    87	## PDF
    88	
    89	**Never** `cat` a PDF — it prints binary garbage.
    90	
    91	Quick first move — get the page count and determine whether the PDF
    92	has an extractable text layer:
    93	
    94	```bash
    95	pdfinfo /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    96	pdffonts /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    97	```
    98	
    99	`pdffonts` tells you whether text extraction will work before you try it:
   100	
   101	- **No fonts listed** (empty table, just the header) → the PDF is a
   102	  scan or raster export. `pdftotext` and `PdfReader.extract_text()`
   103	  will return nothing useful. Go straight to page rasterization or OCR
   104	  — see the `pdf-reading` skill → "Scanned documents".
   105	- **Fonts listed** → there is a text layer; extract it:
   106	  ```bash
   107	  pdftotext -f 1 -l 1 /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf - | head -20
   108	  ```
   109	
   110	The reason to check `pdffonts` first is user-facing: running
   111	`pdftotext` on a scan produces an empty result, and in a visible
   112	transcript that reads as a failed first attempt before you fall back
   113	to OCR. The two-line diagnostic above costs one tool call and avoids
   114	that — you arrive at the right method on the first try, which is what
   115	a user perceives as "it just read my file."
   116	
   117	That also shapes how to open your reply. The diagnostic commands are
   118	plumbing, not content; lead with what the user asked about. On a
   119	scanned receipt that might be "This is a 3-page scanned invoice; the
   120	amount due on page 2 is $1,845.00," and on a digitally-authored report
   121	it might be "The Q3 report runs 28 pages; revenue on p. 4 is $12.3M,
   122	up 9% YoY." What you're steering away from is the "I'll examine the
   123	PDF" / "Let me check if this is extractable" preamble — the answer to
   124	their question is the first thing they should see.
   125	
   126	For anything beyond a quick peek — figures, tables, attachments,
   127	forms, scanned PDFs, visual inspection, or choosing a reading strategy
   128	— go read the `pdf-reading` skill. It covers content inventory, text
   129	extraction vs. page rasterization, embedded content extraction, and
   130	document-type-aware reading strategies.
   131	
   132	For PDF form filling, creation, merging, splitting, or watermarking,
   133	go read the `pdf` skill.
   134	
   135	---
   136	
   137	## DOCX / DOC
   138	
   139	The `docx` skill covers editing, creating, tracked changes, images.
   140	Read it if you need any of those. For a quick look:
   141	
   142	```bash
   143	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/memo.docx | head -200
   144	```
   145	
   146	Legacy `.doc` (not `.docx`) must be converted first — see the `docx`
   147	skill.
   148	
   149	---
   150	
   151	## XLSX / XLS / spreadsheets
   152	
   153	The `xlsx` skill covers formulas, formatting, charts, creating. Read
   154	it if you need any of those. For a quick look at an `.xlsx`:
   155	
   156	```bash
   157	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.xlsx | head -100
   158	```
   159	
   160	For `.xlsm`, add `--format xlsx` (same zip structure; only the
   161	extension differs). When you need a structured preview in Python:
   162	
   163	```python
   164	from openpyxl import load_workbook
   165	wb = load_workbook("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.xlsx", read_only=True)
   166	print("Sheets:", wb.sheetnames)
   167	ws = wb.active
   168	for row in ws.iter_rows(max_row=5, values_only=True):
   169	    print(row)
   170	```
   171	
   172	`read_only=True` matters — without it, openpyxl loads the entire
   173	workbook into memory, which breaks on large files. Do not trust
   174	`ws.max_row` in read-only mode: many non-Excel writers omit the
   175	dimension record, so it comes back `None` or wrong. If you need a row
   176	count, iterate or use pandas.
   177	
   178	**Legacy `.xls`** — openpyxl raises `InvalidFileException`. Use:
   179	
   180	```python
   181	import pandas as pd
   182	df = pd.read_excel("/mnt/user-data/uploads/old.xls", engine="xlrd", nrows=5)
   183	```
   184	
   185	**`.ods` (OpenDocument)** — openpyxl also rejects this. Use:
   186	
   187	```python
   188	import pandas as pd
   189	df = pd.read_excel("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.ods", engine="odf", nrows=5)
   190	```
   191	
   192	---
   193	
   194	## PPTX
   195	
   196	```bash
   197	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/deck.pptx | head -200
   198	```
   199	
   200	**Legacy `.ppt`** — convert to `.pptx` first via LibreOffice; see the
   201	`pptx` skill for the sandbox-safe `scripts/office/soffice.py` wrapper
   202	(bare `soffice` hangs here because the seccomp filter blocks the
   203	`AF_UNIX` sockets LibreOffice uses for instance management).
   204	
   205	For anything beyond reading, go to the `pptx` skill.
   206	
   207	---
   208	
   209	## CSV / TSV
   210	
   211	**Do not** `cat` or `head` these blindly. A CSV with a 50KB quoted cell
   212	in row 1 will wreck your `head -5`. Use pandas with `nrows`:
   213	
   214	```python
   215	import pandas as pd
   216	df = pd.read_csv("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.csv", nrows=5)
   217	print(df)
   218	print()
   219	print(df.dtypes)
   220	```
   221	
   222	Approximate row count without loading (over-counts if the file has
   223	RFC-4180 quoted newlines — the same quoted-cell case this section
   224	warned about above):
   225	
   226	```bash
   227	wc -l /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.csv
   228	```
   229	
   230	Full analysis only after you know the shape:
   231	
   232	```python
   233	df = pd.read_csv("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.csv")
   234	print(df.describe())
   235	```
   236	
   237	TSV: same, with `sep="\t"`.
   238	
   239	---
   240	
   241	## JSON / JSONL
   242	
   243	Structure first, content second:
   244	
   245	```bash
   246	jq 'type' /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.json
   247	jq 'if type == "array" then length elif type == "object" then keys else . end' /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.json
   248	```
   249	
   250	(`keys` errors on scalar JSON roots — a bare `"hello"` or `42` is valid
   251	JSON per RFC 7159 — so guard the branch.)
   252	
   253	Then drill into what the user actually asked about.
   254	
   255	JSONL (one object per line) — do **not** `jq` the whole file; work line
   256	by line:
   257	
   258	```bash
   259	head -3 /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.jsonl | jq .
   260	wc -l /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.jsonl
   261	```
   262	
   263	---
   264	
   265	## Images (JPG / PNG / GIF / WEBP)
   266	
   267	**You can already see uploaded images.** They are injected into your
   268	context as vision inputs alongside the `<uploaded_files>` pointer. You
   269	do not need to read them from disk to describe them.
   270	
   271	The disk copy is only needed if you are going to **process** the image
   272	programmatically:
   273	
   274	```python
   275	from PIL import Image
   276	img = Image.open("/mnt/user-data/uploads/photo.jpg")
   277	print(img.size, img.mode, img.format)
   278	```
   279	
   280	For OCR on an image (text extraction, not description):
   281	
   282	```python
   283	import pytesseract
   284	print(pytesseract.image_to_string(img))
   285	```
   286	
   287	Note: the client resizes images larger than 2000×2000 down to that
   288	bound and re-encodes as JPEG before upload, so the disk copy may not
   289	be the user's original bytes. For most processing this doesn't matter;
   290	if the user is asking about original-resolution pixel data, flag it.
   291	
   292	---
   293	
   294	## Archives (ZIP / TAR / TAR.GZ)
   295	
   296	**List first. Extract never — unless the user explicitly asks.**
   297	Archives can be huge, contain path traversal, or nest forever.
   298	
   299	```bash
   300	unzip -l /mnt/user-data/uploads/bundle.zip
   301	tar -tf /mnt/user-data/uploads/bundle.tar
   302	```
   303	
   304	GNU tar auto-detects compression — `tar -tf` works on `.tar`,
   305	`.tar.gz`, `.tar.bz2`, `.tar.xz` alike. Don't hard-code `-z`.
   306	
   307	If the user wants one file from inside, extract just that one:
   308	
   309	```bash
   310	unzip -p /mnt/user-data/uploads/bundle.zip path/inside/file.txt
   311	```
   312	
   313	**Standalone `.gz`** (not a tar) compresses a single file — there is
   314	no manifest to list. Just peek at the decompressed content:
   315	
   316	```bash
   317	zcat /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.json.gz | head -50
   318	```
   319	
   320	---
   321	
   322	## EPUB / ODT
   323	
   324	```bash
   325	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/book.epub | head -200
   326	```
   327	
   328	For long ebooks, pipe through `head` — you rarely need the whole thing
   329	to answer a question.
   330	
   331	---
   332	
   333	## RTF / IPYNB
   334	
   335	```bash
   336	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/notes.rtf | head -200
   337	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/notebook.ipynb | head -200
   338	```
   339	
   340	---
   341	
   342	## Plain text / code / logs
   343	
   344	Check the size first:
   345	
   346	```bash
   347	wc -c /mnt/user-data/uploads/app.log
   348	```
   349	
   350	- **Under ~20KB**: `cat` is fine.

Here is my assessment, labelled: the findings are measured (139 READ items over Chapters 1–6, the 41 Sweep-B deviations, the Sweep-C line); the severity ranking is my inference from them, on roughly 12 % of the main volume read (L241–1723 of 11,854) plus the 19 chat-62 Mathematical Compendium entries. Nothing below extrapolates to the unread volumes.

**Catastrophic — a false central result, a wrong tower count, a theorem that fails: none found.** Every tower-computable claim re-implemented independently reproduces exactly: 976/1,654/2,535/13,585/70,905/199,130; the closure operator and E = 0 on Λ₈; E(audits) 11/0/19/18/17/16/16; the dimension-2 certificates and the 792 / 4,140 extensions; gcd/lcm = N(a∧b)/N(a∨b) on all 976² pairs; every printed E in Chapter 6's table (36, 20, 106, 0, 0, 0, 7, 0); the covers, the seed, the closed-set counts from chats 65–66. The mathematics the book rests on holds under the strongest test I can apply.

**Critical — would mislead a reader on subject matter if printed as is; publication-blocking, but bounded and each with a determinate fix.** (1) The chat-62 Mathematical Compendium block: 12 of 19 entries with source claims altered without a flag, results printed "Proved" with no Register entry and against the main volume, an overgeneralisation, a substituted measure, two objects merged, one arithmetic error. This is the worst region of the work and the reason for the hold; it is one author, one family, every deviation with a measured source. (2) A handful of main-volume sites: §17.2's classification line true of one class of minima/maxima and false of another with the text silent; "Λ is the same 118 elements" (L1719) for a 976-cell object; ⅅ ≥ 1 printed as "exactly when" where Register 417 says "requires"; Janet's row true only under an unstated convention; a nuclide input called printed that is not, with 80/89 printed against 77/86 reconstructed; about eight measurements with no source anywhere (68 %, 53 %, 39 %/49.5 %, 94 %, the 5→4→3… sequence, Ne II/Ar II/Bi I at D = 5, "three of the twenty-one never fired"). Each must be sourced or withdrawn.

**Serious, not subject-matter — the book's account of itself has drifted from its state.** Stale counts and partial survivals (the withdrawn 1,442 and 2,475; "twenty" for twenty-two; "§2.16 through §2.22"; 13 → 10; "twenty-eight figures" against 32; "eight items" against fourteen; "1/N" beside its own correction; the E(audits) list stopping at three of five), and some fifteen wrong where-pointers (§16.1, Ch. 9, Ch. 10, §25.6, §28.6, §24.2, B.2, §4.6 with no heading, A.4 for A.5, Register 308/286/287 recoverable only from grouped headings). Individually light; collectively they damage exactly the thing the book claims — that it audits itself — and they are the largest class by count. Mechanical to fix once the read is complete, which is why R3 corrects by class.

**Cosmetic / production.** Column dumps and split words on every chapter read so far, four-space paragraphs rendering as code blocks, sub-headings printed as plain lines, "# PART II" inside Chapter 5, §2.22 empty, §2.21–2.24 seated inside Chapter 3, a table header printed twice, the missing references (Hilbert, Gödel, rule of three, Janet, NIST) you have now ruled defects. Unshippable as pages, irrelevant to truth.

So: not catastrophic; critical in one contained region plus a short list of sites; broad but shallow damage to the book's self-consistency; and a production layer that has to be rebuilt anyway. The reading so far has strengthened the core rather than weakened it.

content.text:
Here is my assessment, labelled: the findings are measured (139 READ items over Chapters 1–6, the 41 Sweep-B deviations, the Sweep-C line); the severity ranking is my inference from them, on roughly 12 % of the main volume read (L241–1723 of 11,854) plus the 19 chat-62 Mathematical Compendium entries. Nothing below extrapolates to the unread volumes.

**Catastrophic — a false central result, a wrong tower count, a theorem that fails: none found.** Every tower-computable claim re-implemented independently reproduces exactly: 976/1,654/2,535/13,585/70,905/199,130; the closure operator and E = 0 on Λ₈; E(audits) 11/0/19/18/17/16/16; the dimension-2 certificates and the 792 / 4,140 extensions; gcd/lcm = N(a∧b)/N(a∨b) on all 976² pairs; every printed E in Chapter 6's table (36, 20, 106, 0, 0, 0, 7, 0); the covers, the seed, the closed-set counts from chats 65–66. The mathematics the book rests on holds under the strongest test I can apply.

**Critical — would mislead a reader on subject matter if printed as is; publication-blocking, but bounded and each with a determinate fix.** (1) The chat-62 Mathematical Compendium block: 12 of 19 entries with source claims altered without a flag, results printed "Proved" with no Register entry and against the main volume, an overgeneralisation, a substituted measure, two objects merged, one arithmetic error. This is the worst region of the work and the reason for the hold; it is one author, one family, every deviation with a measured source. (2) A handful of main-volume sites: §17.2's classification line true of one class of minima/maxima and false of another with the text silent; "Λ is the same 118 elements" (L1719) for a 976-cell object; ⅅ ≥ 1 printed as "exactly when" where Register 417 says "requires"; Janet's row true only under an unstated convention; a nuclide input called printed that is not, with 80/89 printed against 77/86 reconstructed; about eight measurements with no source anywhere (68 %, 53 %, 39 %/49.5 %, 94 %, the 5→4→3… sequence, Ne II/Ar II/Bi I at D = 5, "three of the twenty-one never fired"). Each must be sourced or withdrawn.

content.text:
{"returncode":0,"stdout":" 1724| ## 7. The construction of Λ
 1725|  Λ is a set of eight-tuples. Each is a transition cell: a source configuration, a target configuration, and the
 1726|  electron count moved between them.
 1727| 
 1728|       (n, ℓ, k, q, e, f, g, 2S)
 1729| 
 1730| | | |
 1731| |---|---|
 1732| | *n* | source shell |
 1733| | ℓ | source subshell |
 1734| | *k* | source occupancy |
 1735| | *q* | electrons removed |
 1736| | *e* | target shell |
 1737| | *f* | target subshell |
 1738| | *g* | target occupancy |
 1739| | 2*S* | multiplicity |
 1740| 
 1741|  Five further coordinates — 2S′, v, 2J_c, K and 2J — extend Λ₈ to Λ₁₃ when target spin, seniority and
 1742|  angular-momentum coupling are carried explicitly; §12.11 builds the tower and fixes the order, which is
 1743|  J_c, then K, then J. Everything in this book that does not concern coupling is stated for Λ₈.
 1744| 
 1745|  One row of the table below is not like the others. Three origins — Pauli, the hydrogenic solution,
 1746|  counting — yield exact constraints. The fourth, vector coupling, yields an envelope: 2S ≤ k contains
 1747|  every physical multiplicity and admits values no k electrons can carry, at 48.5% density at the caps of
 1748|  §7.4. §12.11.3 states the dichotomy and §12.11.2 proves it is forced.
 1749| 
 1750| ### 7.1 The constraints, and where each comes from
 1751|  Λ is not all of the eight-fold product. It is the subset satisfying:
 1752| 
 1753|   constraint                      origin
 1754|   ℓ≤n−1                           hydrogenic radial solution
 1755|   k ≤ 2(2ℓ + 1)                   Pauli exclusion
 1756|   q≤k                             counting — cannot remove more than are present
 1757|   f≤e−1                           hydrogenic radial solution
 1758|   g ≤ 2(2f + 1)                   Pauli exclusion
 1759|   g≤q                             counting — cannot place more than were removed
 1760|   2S ≤ k                          vector coupling
 1761| 
 1762|  **Seven constraints, four origins, and nothing else.** No constraint in Λ comes from anywhere but Pauli, the hydrogenic radial solution, counting, or angular-momentum coupling. That exhaustiveness matters in Part III, where it is the reason the object's properties can be attributed to *indexing* rather than to physics smuggled in through a bound.
 1763| 
 1764| ### 7.2 Every constraint is of one form
 1765|  Each constraint reads xᵢ ≤ φ(xⱼ) — one coordinate bounded by a monotone function of one other. None is
 1766|  a sum. None is a difference. That is not an accident of presentation; Chapter 17 shows that a sum could
 1767|  not appear here, because a set cut out by a sum bound is not closed.
 1768| 
 1769|  **Consequence, developed in Chapter 8:** the graph whose nodes are coordinates and whose edges are constraints is a **tree**.
 1770| 
 1771| ![Figure 7.1](figures/figure-7.1.png)
 1772| 
 1773|  Figure 7.1. Every constraint binds one coordinate to one other. Eight nodes, seven edges, connected — a tree, and
 1774|  therefore treewidth 1. Three results in this book follow from that fact alone.
 1775| 
 1776| ### 7.3 Λ is closed
 1777|  For any two cells x, y ∈ Λ, both x ∨ y and x ∧ y — the coordinatewise maximum and minimum — are again
 1778|  in Λ.
 1779| 
 1780|  *Proof.* Each constraint is *xᵢ* ≤ φ(*xⱼ*) with φ non-decreasing. Suppose (*x*∨*y*)ᵢ = *xᵢ*. Then
 1781| 
 1782|     (x∨y)ᵢ = xᵢ ≤ φ(xⱼ) ≤ φ(max(xⱼ, yⱼ)) = φ((x∨y)ⱼ)
 1783| 
 1784|  by monotonicity. Meets are symmetric. ∎

# READ-ch7 — Phase R2, main volume Chapter 7 "The construction of Λ" (chat 70)

Member The_Method_1_6-2.md (BUILD90 main, md5 4aef772b…), L1724–L1795 (72 lines), read in full against (i) each cited section, (ii) the rebuilt tower (tower-2.py, c0bce27a…), (iii) the chapter instrument r2-ch7.py (beside tower-2.py) and the clerical checker r2-tools.py. Rulings applied: A vocabulary; an unreferenced prior-art attribution is a defect; a co-located stale figure counts against its census row. The chapter has **no census rows** (r2-tools.py census 1724 1795 → 0); CENSUS-CLOSURES-ch7.tsv is the header alone.

## A. Deviations (both texts)

**7-01 · L1790 (§7.4), with L1800, L1849, L1875, L1883 (Ch. 8) and L3065 (§12.11.5).** PRINTED L1790: `every count in this book is stated at explicit caps on n, e, ℓ and k` — four coordinates. PRINTED L1800: `(n_max, e_max, ℓ_max, k_max, f_max) = (3, 3, 1, 3, 1)` — five. PRINTED L1849, L1875, L1883: `At caps (3,3,1,3), k ≥ 1` — four. PRINTED L3065: `f_max — the cap on f under §7.4` — attributes to §7.4 a cap §7.4 does not name. MEASURED (r2-ch7.py): the seven constraints of §7.1 at (n, e, ℓ, k) ≤ (3, 3, 1, 3), k ≥ 1 give **1,176** cells with f bounded only by f ≤ e−1, and **976** only with f ≤ 1 added; k ≥ 0 instead of k ≥ 1 gives 1,001. READING: the object's defining count cannot be rebuilt from §7.1 and §7.4 as printed; the fifth cap is stated once (L1800) and cited back to a section that omits it. Defect (definition under-specified at its home; four-tuple and five-tuple cap statements coexist). Correction site: §7.4's list (add f, or "the two subshell coordinates ℓ and f"), and the three four-tuples in Chapter 8 to match L1800. For R3.

**7-02 · L1786 (§7.3).** PRINTED: `verified by direct computation at four cap settings — 216, 976, 1,636 and 2,394 cells`. SOURCE: 2,394 has no second site in any volume (r2-tools.py figures); 216 and 1,636 recur at L3975 and Register L2225 as the ends of a range for a different test (seed necessity), not as E-sites. MEASURED (r2-ch7.py): the settings are (n, e, ℓ, f, k) = (2,2,1,0,3) [216, one of 60 settings giving that count], (3,3,1,1,3) [976], (3,3,1,1,4) [1,636], (4,3,1,1,4) [2,394]; **E = 0 at all four, first pass +0, second pass +0** — the claim reproduces. READING: not a false claim; the settings are not printed beside the figures although Chapter 8 L1798–1800 promises "where a figure is recomputed under variation the settings are printed beside it". Not a defect on the ruled classes; incidental gap for the prose pass (print the four settings).

**7-03 · L1773–1774 (Figure 7.1 caption) and L5150.** PRINTED L1774: `Three results in this book follow from that fact alone.` — the three are not named at the site or anywhere the phrase is cited. PRINTED L5150 (Ch. 18): `Λ's own shape, which §7.1 says three central results follow from` — the caption sits under §7.2 (L1764), not §7.1. MEASURED (grep `treewidth`, 8 sites): candidates are exact closure at treewidth 1 (§18.4.1, L2863), the tree factorisation of the void count (A.10, L?), and arc-consistency sufficiency at treewidth 1 (L5693). INFERRED: the enumeration is owed. Named-statement without its list; pointer §7.1 → §7.2 wrong by one subsection. Not subject-matter; for the prose pass.

**7-04 · L1792 (§7.4).** PRINTED: `identical across a twenty-eight-fold range in cell count`. SOURCE Ch. 8 L1928: `six settings from 976 to 27,873 cells`. MEASURED: 27,873 / 976 = 28.56. READING: "twenty-eight-fold" is a floor of 28.6; the top setting 27,873 was not reached by any (n, e ≤ 5; ℓ, f ≤ 3; k ≤ 8) setting of the §7.1 constraints (r2-ch7.py grid) — Chapter 8's settings to be read in its own segment. Carried to Ch. 8.

**7-05 · L1728, L1782 (layout).** Four-space-indented display lines `(n, ℓ, k, q, e, f, g, 2S)` and the join inequality render as code blocks; L1753–1760 is a space-aligned column dump (the constraint table). MEASURED (r2-tools.py layout). Production; same class as READ-ch3 3-31.

## B. Verified (claim and source agree; instrument where one exists)

- L1751–1760 the seven constraints: identical to tower-2.py's L8() (MEASURED, set equality of 976 cells rebuilt from the printed text).
- L1762 "seven constraints, four origins": 7 rows; origins hydrogenic ×2, Pauli ×2, counting ×2, vector coupling ×1 = 4 (MEASURED).
- L1741–1743 five further coordinates 2S′, v, 2J_c, K, 2J in that order; coupling order J_c, K, J: matches tower-2.py's stage order (2S′, v, 2J_c, 2K, 2J) and §12.11.1's table L2941–2942 (axis named K, bound 2K ≤ 2J_c + 2f_max) (MEASURED).
- L1745–1748 three exact origins and one envelope: §12.11.3 L3394 "Counting coordinates close exactly. Coupling coordinates close as envelopes" (MEASURED text); §12.11.2 as the proof — record-carried to Ch. 12.
- L1747 "48.5 % density": cells whose 2S a k-electron subshell of capacity 4ℓ+2 can carry (2S ≡ k mod 2, 2S ≤ min(k, 4ℓ+2−k)) = 473 of 976 = 48.46 % (MEASURED; definition INFERRED from physics, match exact to rounding); 503 cells carry a 2S no k electrons can — "admits values no k electrons can carry" (MEASURED).
- L1765 every constraint xᵢ ≤ φ(xⱼ), φ non-decreasing, none a sum or difference: by inspection of the seven (MEASURED); sums fail closure 0 of 28 pairs (minmax.py, chat 66 instrument; MEASURED); Chapter 17 L4870–4880 carries the worked sum case g₁ + g₂ ≤ q and §17.2's "sums, products and differences do not" (MEASURED text).
- L1769, L1773 the constraint graph is a tree: 8 nodes, 7 edges, connected (MEASURED, r2-ch7.py); treewidth 1 follows (INFERRED, standard).
- L1780–1784 the closure proof: correct for joins as printed; for meets, (x∧y)ᵢ = min(xᵢ, yᵢ) ≤ φ(min(xⱼ, yⱼ)) holds by the same monotonicity with the roles exchanged — "Meets are symmetric" is right (INFERRED, checked).
- L1786 E(Λ) = 0 at four settings: see 7-02, reproduced.
- L1790–1791 counts change with caps, shape does not: Ch. 8 L1928 states the invariance under six settings — record-carried to Ch. 8.
- L1794 "checked at no fewer than four settings": consistent with L1786 (four) and Ch. 8 (six).
- Pointers: §12.11 → L2524, §7.4 → L1789, §12.11.3 → L3394, §12.11.2 → L3363, Ch. 17 → L4789, Ch. 8 → L1796, Figure 7.1 placed at L1771 — all resolve to headings carrying the cited matter (MEASURED, r2-tools.py pointers).

## C. Incidental

- Figure 7.1's file `figures/figure-7.1.png` is not a bundle member; existence at press is a production check (the constraint-graph figure exists in the project files as fig5_constraint_graphs.png).
- The global constants check (r2-tools.py constants, all six volumes): 976 at 175 sites, 1,654 at 42, 2,535 at 15, 13,585 at 12, 70,905 at 15, 199,130 at 30, 475,800 at 19; no off-by-one variant of any tower value anywhere; '975' at Register L1729, L3627 and IoI L1355 and '977' at Register L3635, L3885 are to be read in place in those volumes' segments.

 1810|  **§32.4.2's distinction is why this matters** — every one of those 69 carries a *value* rather than an
 1811|  identity, and a value without its setting is a reading whose conditions are missing. Register 395.
 1812| 
 1813| ### 8.1 Distributive
 1814|  Λ is a sublattice of a product of chains, and every such sublattice is distributive. Verified on 4,000
 1815|  randomly drawn triples, no failures.
 1816| 
 1817|  This is the least surprising fact in the chapter and the most load-bearing: it is what admits Birkhoff's representation, which is the next section.
 1818| 
 1819| ### 8.2 Rank is conserved
 1820|  Λ has a conservation law, and it is exact.
 1821| 
 1822|     rank(a ∨ b) + rank(a ∧ b) = rank(a) + rank(b)
 1823| 
 1824|  **Verified on all 475,800 pairs: zero violations.**
 1825| 
 1826|  **This is modularity, and it is strictly stronger than what most rank functions satisfy.** Matroid rank is *sub*modular — the left side is ≤ the right. Entropy is submodular. **Λ's rank is modular, with equality, and that equality is the signature of distributivity.**
 1827| 
 1828| ### 8.2.1 What it means
 1829|  Join and meet redistribute rank without creating or destroying it. Taking the join of two cells
 1830|  raises the rank by exactly what taking the meet lowers it. A quantity is conserved by the lattice's
 1831|  operations, in the way energy is conserved by a canonical transformation.
 1832| 
 1833|  **The question came from outside the subject.** Celestial mechanics is organised around invariants — the Jacobi integral, angular momentum, energy — and asking *what does Λ conserve* is not a question a spectroscopist would think to put. **This book had not put it.**
 1834| 
 1835| ### 8.2.2 And it is a cheaper test than §8.1's
 1836|  §8.1 verifies distributivity by checking a ∧ (b ∨ c) = (a∧b) ∨ (a∧c) over triples — O(n³).

 1838|  equivalent:
 1839| 
 1840| | test | sample | time |
 1841| |---|---|---|
 1842| | distributive law, triples | 4,000 | 0.0375 s |

 1844| 
 1845|  **Both true. The second is the one to run first**, because a failure of modularity is a failure of distributivity and it is found in half the work.
 1846|

 1848|  By Birkhoff's theorem, a finite distributive lattice is the lattice of down-sets of its poset of join-irreducibles.
 1849|  For Λ at caps (3,3,1,3), k ≥ 1:
 1850| 
 1851|     976 cells ← 17 join-irreducibles, 20 covering relations
 1852| 
 1853|  and the correspondence is exact: **all 976 down-sets of the 17-element poset are precisely the 976 cells.** A fifty-seven-fold compression.
 1854| 
 1855|  **The covering relations are the physics made visible:**
 1856| 
 1857| | cover | reads |
 1858| |---|---|
 1859| | *e*=2 ⋖ *e*=2, *f*=1 | a target subshell requires its shell |
 1860| | *k*=2 ⋖ *k*=2, *q*=2 | you may remove what you have |
 1861| | *n*=2 ⋖ *n*=2, ℓ=1 ⋖ *n*=2, ℓ=1, *k*=3 | shell before subshell before occupancy |
 1862|

 1866|

 1868| 
 1869|  Figure 8.1. The seventeen join-irreducibles and their twenty covering relations. Every one of the 976 cells is a down-set
 1870|  of this poset, and every down-set is a cell — a fifty-seven-fold compression, exact. The covers are the constraints of §7.1
","stderr":""}

 1872| 
 1873| ### 8.4 Sperner, and not symmetric
 1874|  The largest antichain in Λ equals its largest rank level — the Sperner property — verified exactly at five
 1875|  cap settings by Dilworth's theorem and bipartite matching, no exceptions. At caps (3,3,1,3), k ≥ 1 the maximum
 1876|  is 122 at rank 11.
 1877| 
 1878|  The rank sequence is **log-concave**, hence unimodal, which is why Sperner holds rather than merely happening to.
 1879| 
 1880|  **But Λ is not rank-symmetric**, so it has **no symmetric chain decomposition** and the classical result for divisor lattices does not transfer. The asymmetry is itself a measurement:
 1881| 
 1882|     centre of mass 11.07 against midpoint 11.5 — skew −0.43, computed from the full rank sequence
 1883|     at caps (3,3,1,3), k ≥ 1, over all 976 cells
 1884| 
 1885|  Low ranks are cut by floors (*n* ≥ 1, *k* ≥ 1, *e* ≥ 1); high ranks by caps (ℓ ≤ *n*−1, *k* ≤ 2(2ℓ+1), *q* ≤ *k*, *g* ≤ *q*). **There are more caps than floors, so the top is pruned harder.** The skew is how much more Pauli constrains than counting does.
 1886| 
 1887|  Nor is Λ self-dual. Only 8 of 976 cells survive the reflection x ↦ max − x, coordinate by coordinate —
 1888|  reproduced exactly on recomputation. The tower session's competing figure of 112 was computed under
 1889|  x ↦ max + min − x, a different map, which the floors n ≥ 1, k ≥ 1, e ≥ 1 separate from this one; under
 1890|  that map 112 cells have their image in Λ and none is fixed. Both counts are right about their own
 1891|  reflection. The discrepancy was definitional, and it is closed. This reflection is not decoration: restricted to
 1892|  one occupancy coordinate it is particle-hole conjugation, terms(ℓᵏ) = terms(ℓ^(4ℓ+2−k)) exactly, and
 1893|  §12.11.2 shows it is one of the three machines that price every coupling axis. The
 1894|  two sides of the object are genuinely distinguishable, which Chapter 12 develops.
 1895| 
 1896| ![Figure 8.2](figures/figure-8.2.png)
 1897| 
 1898|  Figure 8.2. The rank sequence over all 976 cells is log-concave, hence unimodal, hence Sperner. It is not symmetric: the
 1899|  centre of mass sits below the midpoint by 0.43, because Λ has more caps than floors.
 1900| 
 1901| ### 8.5 The constraint graph is a tree
 1902|  Eight coordinates, seven constraints, connected:
 1903| 
 1904|     e — f — g — q — k — ℓ — n, with 2S attached to k
 1905| 
 1906|  **Treewidth 1.** Three consequences run through the rest of the book:
 1907| 
 1908|  **The void needs no sieve.** A tree has no cycles, so there is nothing for inclusion–exclusion to correct. Chapter 10 gives the closed-form count.
 1909| 
 1910|  **The order is recoverable.** Chapter 15 recovers Λ's coordinate orders from an unlabelled bag of cells by propagation along this tree — 20 of 20.
 1911| 
 1912|  **And the constraint graph offers no redundancy.** There is exactly one path between any two nodes. So the two-route protection of Chapter 16 cannot come from the constraints; it must come from derived quantities. **That is a real constraint on how the object defends itself, and it is visible here, three chapters early.**
 1913| 
 1914| ### 8.6 Order dimension
 1915|  Λ₈ has order dimension exactly **7**. Seven linear orders rebuild the partial order, and no six can.
 1916|  The eight-coordinate construction gives dim ≤ 8 for free; the eighth is never spent.
 1917| 
 1918|  **The figure printed here through every earlier build was 8, asserted rather than derived — register
 1919|  409 flagged it as the one quantity in Part II carried without a derivation — and the derivation,
 1920|  now run, corrects it.** The order dimension of a finite distributive lattice is the width of its
 1921|  poset of join-irreducibles — Dilworth — and §8.3's seventeen generators have width **seven**,
 1922|  certified both ways: a partition of the seventeen into seven chains, and seven of them pairwise
 1923|  incomparable — one generator for each coordinate except *g*. The generator that first raises *g* is
 1924|  (1,0,1,1,1,0,1,0), and it sits above the generator that first raises *q*, because g ≤ q: **you cannot
 1925|  raise the coupling without having already raised what it couples.** Every g-raising generator lies
 1926|  above the q-atom, so *g* contributes no independent member to any antichain of generators, and the
 1927|  order pays seven dimensions for eight axes. The coordinates remain irredundant in value — no axis is
 1928|  a function of the others — but in order, *g*'s information rides on *q*'s. Λ₉ measures width 7 as
 1929|  well, so the dimension does not rise by one per adjoined axis; it rises when the new axis brings an
 1930|  independent generator, and a coupled axis need not. This is register 36's method — exhibit the
 1931|  antichain, or fail to — run at last past three coordinates, and the one underived number in Part II
 1932|  is the one it refutes. Register 409.
 1933| 
 1934|  Λ occupies **14.1%** of its own bounding box — 976 cells of 6,912.
 1935|

# usage: python3 r2-ch8.py            (core claims)
#        python3 r2-ch8.py settings   (search for the six settings 976 … 27,873 and generator counts where affordable)
import itertools, importlib.util, sys, random, collections
import numpy as np
spec=importlib.util.spec_from_file_location('tower','tower-2.py'); tw=importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec); spec.loader.exec_module(tw)

def leq_matrix(A):
    """A: (n,d) int array. returns boolean n×n matrix LE[i,j] = A[i] ≤ A[j] coordinatewise"""
    n=len(A); LE=np.ones((n,n),dtype=bool)
    for c in range(A.shape[1]): LE &= (A[:,c][:,None] <= A[:,c][None,:])
    return LE

def join_irreducibles(A):
    """elements with exactly one lower cover (bottom excluded). returns indices, and the list of lower covers per element"""
    n=len(A); LE=leq_matrix(A); LT=LE & ~np.eye(n,dtype=bool)
    ji=[]; 
    for x in range(n):
        below=np.nonzero(LT[:,x])[0]
        if len(below)==0: continue                       # bottom
        # lower covers: y below x with no z strictly between
        sub=LT[np.ix_(below,below)]                        # sub[i,j] = below[i] < below[j]
        maximal=below[~sub.any(axis=1)]
        if len(maximal)==1: ji.append(x)

    matchR=[-1]*n; INF=10**9
    def bfs():
        dist=[0 if matchL[u]==-1 else INF for u in range(n)]; q=collections.deque(u for u in range(n) if matchL[u]==-1); found=False
        while q:
            u=q.popleft()
            for v in adj[u]:
                w=matchR[v]
                if w==-1: found=True
                elif dist[w]==INF: dist[w]=dist[u]+1; q.append(w)
        return found,dist
    def dfs(u,dist):
        for v in adj[u]:
            w=matchR[v]
            if w==-1 or (dist[w]==dist[u]+1 and dfs(w,dist)):
                matchL[u]=v; matchR[v]=u; return True

for a,b in [((1,0,1,0,2,0,0,0),(1,0,1,0,2,1,0,0)),((1,0,2,0,1,0,0,0),(1,0,2,2,1,0,0,0)),((2,0,1,0,1,0,0,0),(2,1,1,0,1,0,0,0)),((2,1,1,0,1,0,0,0),(2,1,3,0,1,0,0,0))]:

print('|Λ9|',len(L9),'join-irreducibles',len(ji9),'width(J(Λ9)) =',width_dilworth(LEJ9 & ~np.eye(len(ji9),dtype=bool)))

    for s in [(3,3,1,1,3),(3,3,1,1,4),(4,3,1,1,4),(4,4,1,1,4),(3,3,1,1,5),(4,4,1,1,3)]:

# READ-ch8 — Phase R2, main volume Chapter 8 "What Λ is — distributive, modular, Sperner" (chat 70)

Member The_Method_1_6-2.md (BUILD90 main, md5 4aef772b…), L1796–L1935 (140 lines), read in full against (i) each cited section and Register entry, (ii) the rebuilt tower (tower-2.py, c0bce27a…), (iii) the chapter instrument r2-ch8.py (beside tower-2.py; `settings` mode for the cap ladder) and r2-tools.py. Rulings applied as in READ-ch7. Census rows in range: 1048, 1049 (closed in CENSUS-CLOSURES-ch8.tsv).

## A. Deviations (both texts)

**8-01 · L1863 (§8.3) against L1799–1802 (the chapter's own convention).** PRINTED: `Across six settings from 976 to 27,873 cells the generator count grows — 17, 23, 31, 32 — while the *patterns* hold at fifteen, with zero new and zero lost.` SOURCE: 27,873 has no other site in any volume; no site prints the six settings; four counts are listed for six settings; "patterns" is not defined at the site or elsewhere by grep. MEASURED (r2-ch8.py settings; ji_fast): 27,873 cells is the setting (n, e, ℓ, f, k) = (6,5,2,2,5), unique in n,e ≤ 6, ℓ,f ≤ 2, k ≤ 8; join-irreducible counts **17 at 976 (3,3,1,1,3), 23 at 3,363 (4,4,1,1,4), 31 at 21,775 (5,5,2,2,5), 32 at 27,873 (6,5,2,2,5)** — all four printed values reproduce at natural settings (settings INFERRED as the book's; values MEASURED). READING: the values are true; the settings are not printed beside the figure although L1801 says they are, two of the six settings and their counts are absent, and "fifteen patterns" is unverifiable as printed. Not a false claim; a stated-convention breach at the site that states the convention. For the prose pass: print the six settings and their six counts, define "pattern".

**8-02 · L1837–1838 (§8.2.2).** PRINTED: `on a graded lattice with this rank function it [modularity of rank] is equivalent [to distributivity]`. INFERRED (standard): rank-modularity is equivalent to lattice modularity, not to distributivity — M₃ is graded, its rank satisfies r(a∨b) + r(a∧b) = r(a) + r(b) on every pair, and it is not distributive. The direction the section uses (L1845 "a failure of modularity is a failure of distributivity") is correct; "equivalent" overstates it. For a sublattice of a product of chains with rank Σxᵢ both properties hold outright (MEASURED here), so nothing computed is affected. Wording overclaim in a mathematical statement; correction: "necessary" (or "equivalent to modularity"). For R3, low.

**8-03 · L1874–1875 (§8.4).** PRINTED: `verified exactly at five cap settings by Dilworth's theorem and bipartite matching`. SOURCE: the five settings are not named. MEASURED (r2-ch8.py, Hopcroft–Karp on the comparability graph): width = largest rank level at (2,2,1,0,3) 29 = 29, (3,3,1,1,3) 122 = 122, (3,3,1,1,4) 160 = 160; log-concave at all three. Reproduced where tested; the other two settings unnamed. Same class as 8-01; for the prose pass.

**8-04 · L1849, L1875, L1883.** `At caps (3,3,1,3), k ≥ 1` — four-tuples against the five-tuple convention stated at L1800 in the same chapter. Already recorded as READ-ch7 7-01 (defect); no separate closure.

**8-05 · L1804–1806, L1822, L1851, L1882–1883, L1904 (layout).** Four-space-indented display lines render as code blocks; L1863 table and L1857–1861 fine. MEASURED (r2-tools.py layout). Production.

## B. Verified (claim and source agree; instrument where one exists — all MEASURED unless marked)

- L1800 the caps (3,3,1,3,1) rebuild Λ₈ to 976 (READ-ch7).
- L1808–1809 "84 paragraphs … 69 name no cap … 82 %": 69/84 = 82.1 %; Register 395 (R L1467) records exactly these figures — record-carried.
- L1814 distributive: sublattice of a product of chains (INFERRED, standard); 20,000 random triples, 0 failures.
- L1822–1824 rank modularity on all 475,800 = C(976,2) pairs: 0 violations.
- L1836 O(n³) vs O(n²), L1842–1843 timings 0.0375 s / 0.0188 s "half the work": 0.0188/0.0375 = 0.50 (arithmetic); timings themselves not reproducible.
- L1851–1853 976 cells ← 17 join-irreducibles, 20 covering relations; all 976 down-sets of the 17-element poset are the 976 cells; 976/17 = 57.4 "fifty-seven-fold": all reproduced (down-sets counted by enumeration of the 2¹⁷ subsets).
- L1857–1861 the four printed covers e=2 ⋖ e=2,f=1; k=2 ⋖ k=2,q=2; n=2 ⋖ n=2,ℓ=1 ⋖ n=2,ℓ=1,k=3: each pair both join-irreducible and a cover in J(Λ₈).
- L1876 maximum 122 at rank 11: rank sequence [1, 5, 15, 34, 59, 87, 108, 121, 122, 115, 100, 79, 57, 37, 21, 10, 4, 1] over ranks 3–20; L1878 log-concave hence unimodal: true.
- L1880 not rank-symmetric: true; no symmetric chain decomposition follows (INFERRED, standard).
- L1882 centre of mass 11.07, midpoint 11.5, skew −0.43: 11.07 / 11.5 / −0.43 exactly.
- L1885 floors n, k, e ≥ 1 and caps: min (1,0,1,0,1,0,0,0), max (3,1,3,3,3,1,3,3) — the three floors and the listed caps are the binding ones.
- L1887–1890 8 of 976 cells survive x ↦ max − x; 112 have their image in Λ under x ↦ max + min − x and none is fixed: 8 / 112 / 0.
- L1892 particle–hole conjugation terms(ℓᵏ) = terms(ℓ^(4ℓ+2−k)): standard (INFERRED). §12.11.2 as one of three machines — record-carried to Ch. 12.
- L1902–1904 tree e — f — g — q — k — ℓ — n with 2S on k: the seven edges of READ-ch7 (MEASURED).
- L1908 Ch. 10 closed-form void count; L1910 Ch. 15 order recovery 20 of 20; L1912 Ch. 16 two-route protection — record-carried to their chapters.
- L1915 order dimension 7, seven linear orders and no six: width(J(Λ₈)) = 7 by Dilworth (matching), maximum antichain of seven exhibited — one generator per coordinate except g: (3,0,1,0,1,0,0,0) n, (2,1,1,0,1,0,0,0) ℓ, (1,0,2,0,1,0,0,0) k, (1,0,1,1,1,0,0,0) q, (1,0,1,0,3,0,0,0) e, (1,0,1,0,2,1,0,0) f, (1,0,1,0,1,0,0,1) 2S. Dimension = width of J for a finite distributive lattice: standard (INFERRED); confirmed by HANDOFF-20's carried width 7.
- L1923–1926 the g-atom (1,0,1,1,1,0,1,0) is join-irreducible and lies above the q-atom (1,0,1,1,1,0,0,0): true.
- L1928 Λ₉ measures width 7: |Λ₉| = 1,654, 20 join-irreducibles, width(J(Λ₉)) = 7.
- L1918–1919, L1932 Register 409 (R L1523) "dim(Λ₈) = 8 was asserted and is Dilworth's, being the width of J(Λ)": as cited. L1930 Register 36 (R L215) exhibits S₃ within Λ — the "exhibit the antichain" method: as cited.
- L1934 976 of 6,912 = 14.1 %: box = 3·2·3·4·3·2·4·4 = 6,912; 14.12 %.
- Pointers §6.2.1, §12.11.1.1, §12.11.1.2, §22.1.1.1, §32.4.2, §8.1, §8.3, §7.1, §12.11.2, Ch. 10/12/15/16, Figures 8.1 and 8.2 (placed L1867, L1896): all resolve to headings carrying the cited matter (r2-tools.py pointers).

## C. Incidental

- Census 1048 ("had never been written down"): Register 395 states it in the same words — not a defect. Census 1049 ("the eighth is never spent"): dim = 7 < 8 measured — not a defect.
- The generator-count ladder (MEASURED, ji_fast): 976→17, 1,636→21, 1,968→19, 2,394→22, 2,680→25, 3,363→23, 4,428→24, 6,739→25, 9,520→29, 12,451→27, 15,885→28, 21,775→31, 27,873→32, 57,645→37 — banked for whoever prints the six settings.

# r2-ch9.py — Phase R2, main Chapter 9 "The arithmetic encoding" (chat 70). Run beside tower-2.py.
import importlib.util, itertools, random, math, collections
import numpy as np
spec=importlib.util.spec_from_file_location('tower','tower-2.py'); tw=importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec); spec.loader.exec_module(tw)
cells=tw.L8(); S=set(cells); n=len(cells); A=np.array(cells,dtype=np.int16)
P=[2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19]
def N(x):
    v=1
    for p,e in zip(P,x): v*=p**e
    return v
def Omega(m):
    c=0
    for p in P:
        while m%p==0: m//=p; c+=1
    return c
def omega(m): return sum(1 for p in P if m%p==0)
def tau(m):
    t=1
    for p in P:
        e=0
        while m%p==0: m//=p; e+=1
        t*=e+1
    return t
Nv=[N(x) for x in cells]
print('rank = Ω(N) on all cells:',all(sum(x)==Omega(v) for x,v in zip(cells,Nv)),'| ω ≤ 8 on all:',max(omega(v) for v in Nv)<=8,'| cell (2,1,3,3,2,1,3,3) in Λ:',(2,1,3,3,2,1,3,3) in S,'ω there:',omega(N((2,1,3,3,2,1,3,3))),'| cells with ω = 8:',sum(omega(v)==8 for v in Nv))
# gcd/lcm = meet/join on all pairs; divisibility = order
bad=0; comp=0
for i in range(n):
    for j in range(i+1,n):
        x,y=cells[i],cells[j]; a,b=Nv[i],Nv[j]; g=math.gcd(a,b)
        if N(tuple(map(min,x,y)))!=g or N(tuple(map(max,x,y)))!=a*b//g: bad+=1
        if (all(p<=q for p,q in zip(x,y)) != (b%a==0)) or (all(q<=p for p,q in zip(x,y)) != (a%b==0)): bad+=1
        if all(p<=q for p,q in zip(x,y)) or all(q<=p for p,q in zip(x,y)): comp+=1
pairs=n*(n-1)//2
print(f'gcd/lcm = meet/join and divisibility = order on all {pairs} pairs: violations {bad} | comparable pairs {comp} = {100*comp/pairs:.1f}% of pairs')
# the five forms of d
def interval_cells(x,y):
    lo=tuple(map(min,x,y)); hi=tuple(map(max,x,y))
    return sum(1 for z in itertools.product(*[range(l,h+1) for l,h in zip(lo,hi)]) if z in S)
def box(x,y): return math.prod(abs(p-q)+1 for p,q in zip(x,y))
random.seed(1); eq12=0; eq23=0; eq24=0; eq25=0; tot=0; voidbearing=0
for _ in range(2000):
    x=random.choice(cells); y=random.choice(cells); a,b=N(x),N(y); g=math.gcd(a,b)
    f1=interval_cells(x,y); f2=box(x,y); f3=tau(a*b//(g*g)); f4=tau((a//g)*(b//g)); f5=math.prod(abs(p-q)+1 for p,q in zip(x,y))
    tot+=1; eq12+=(f1==f2); eq23+=(f2==f3); eq24+=(f2==f4); eq25+=(f2==f5); voidbearing+=(f1!=f2)
print(f'2,000 random pairs: form1 (Λ-interval count) = form2 (∏(|Δ|+1)) in {eq12}; form2=form3 {eq23}; form2=form4 {eq24}; form2=form5 {eq25}; pairs whose box holds a non-cell (void-bearing) {voidbearing}')
# exhaustive: how many of all pairs have a void in their box?
def boxfree(x,y):
    lo=tuple(map(min,x,y)); hi=tuple(map(max,x,y))
    # seven comparisons: the box is in Λ iff every constraint holds at its worst corner (hi on the bounded side, lo on the bounding side)
    return (hi[1]<=lo[0]-1 and hi[2]<=4*lo[1]+2 and hi[3]<=lo[2] and hi[5]<=lo[4]-1 and hi[6]<=4*lo[5]+2 and hi[6]<=lo[3] and hi[7]<=lo[2])
# validate the seven-comparison test against brute force on 3,000 pairs
ok=all(boxfree(x,y)==(interval_cells(x,y)==box(x,y)) for x,y in ((random.choice(cells),random.choice(cells)) for _ in range(3000)))
print('seven-comparison void-free test agrees with brute force on 3,000 pairs:',ok)
vf=sum(boxfree(cells[i],cells[j]) for i in range(n) for j in range(i+1,n)); print(f'void-free boxes over all {pairs} pairs: {vf} ({100*vf/pairs:.1f}%); void-bearing {pairs-vf}')
# triangle inequality, log d metric checks
viol=0
for _ in range(4000):
    x,y,z=(random.choice(cells) for _ in range(3))
    if box(x,z)>box(x,y)*box(y,z): viol+=1
print('multiplicative triangle inequality on 4,000 triples: violations',viol,'| d(x,x)=1:',box(cells[5],cells[5])==1)
# join-irreducible representation for the Möbius closed form
LE=np.ones((n,n),dtype=bool)
for c in range(8): LE&=(A[:,c][:,None]<=A[:,c][None,:])
LT=LE&~np.eye(n,dtype=bool)
ji=[x for x in range(n) if LT[:,x].any() and (lambda b:(~LT[np.ix_(b,b)].any(axis=1)).sum()==1)(np.nonzero(LT[:,x])[0])]
m=len(ji); rep=[frozenset(j for j in ji if LE[j,x]) for x in range(n)]     # JI below each cell
jiLT={(a,b):bool(LT[a,b]) for a in ji for b in ji}
def mu_closed(x,y):
    D=rep[y]-rep[x]
    if any(jiLT[(a,b)] for a in D for b in D): return 0
    return (-1)**len(D)
idx={c:i for i,c in enumerate(cells)}
def mu_rec(x,y,memo):
    if x==y: return 1
    if (x,y) in memo: return memo[(x,y)]
    lo=cells[x]; hi=cells[y]
    zs=[idx[z] for z in itertools.product(*[range(l,h+1) for l,h in zip(lo,hi)]) if z in S and z!=hi]
    v=-sum(mu_rec(x,z,memo) for z in zs); memo[(x,y)]=v; return v
random.seed(2); cmp_pairs=[(i,j) for i in range(n) for j in range(n) if LT[i,j]]
sample=random.sample(cmp_pairs,300); memo={}
agree=sum(mu_closed(i,j)==mu_rec(i,j,memo) for i,j in sample)
print(f'join-irreducibles {m}; Möbius closed form = recursive definition on {agree} of 300 sampled comparable pairs; values ⊆ {{-1,0,1}}:',set(mu_closed(i,j) for i,j in cmp_pairs)<= {-1,0,1})
# μ_Λ = μ_arith iff void-free unit hypercube — on ALL comparable pairs
def mu_arith(x,y):
    d=[q-p for p,q in zip(x,y)]
    return 0 if any(e>=2 for e in d) else (-1)**sum(d)
cnt=collections.Counter()
for i,j in cmp_pairs:
    x,y=cells[i],cells[j]; unit=all(q-p<=1 for p,q in zip(x,y)); vfree=boxfree(x,y); ag=(mu_closed(i,j)==mu_arith(x,y))
    cnt[(unit,vfree,ag)]+=1
print('all comparable pairs (unit-hypercube?, void-free?, μ_Λ = μ_arith?) →',dict(cnt))

# READ-ch9 — Phase R2, main volume Chapter 9 "The arithmetic encoding" (chat 70)

Member The_Method_1_6-2.md (BUILD90 main, md5 4aef772b…), L1936–L2020 (85 lines), read in full against (i) each cited section and Register entry, (ii) the rebuilt tower (tower-2.py, c0bce27a…), (iii) the chapter instrument r2-ch9.py (beside tower-2.py) and r2-tools.py. Rulings applied as in READ-ch7. Census rows in range: none; CENSUS-CLOSURES-ch9.tsv is the header alone.

## A. Deviations (both texts)

**9-01 · L2019 (§9.3) — a stated biconditional that is false in general.** PRINTED: `μ_Λ = μ_arith **iff** the interval is a void-free unit hypercube. Exact — 60 void-free pairs all agree, 56 void-bearing pairs all disagree, no mixed case.` MEASURED (r2-ch9.py, all 115,162 comparable pairs of Λ₈; μ_Λ by the closed form of L2015, itself verified against the recursive definition on 300 of 300 sampled pairs; μ_arith = the number-theoretic Möbius function of N(y)/N(x)): void-free unit hypercubes 18,103 — all agree; void-bearing unit hypercubes 17,104 — all disagree; **non-unit intervals (some Δᵢ ≥ 2) 79,955 — all agree, both functions being 0** (13,501 void-free, 66,454 void-bearing). Agreement therefore holds on 98,058 of 115,162 comparable pairs, not only on void-free unit hypercubes. READING: the 116 tested pairs were evidently all unit hypercubes, and the biconditional was stated for the whole lattice. True statement: *restricted to unit-hypercube intervals*, μ_Λ = μ_arith iff the interval is void-free; on every non-unit interval both vanish. Defect, subject-matter (an "Exact" theorem overgeneralised from its sample). For R3: restate with the restriction; a Register correction entry (both states kept).

**9-02 · L1996–2002 (§9.2 "Five equivalent forms") with L1994 and the Figure 9.1 caption L2009.** PRINTED: form 1 `|[x∧y, x∨y]| — interval count`; L1994 `The measure counts *cells*, and a cell is occupied`; L2009 `d(x,y) counts cells in the interval between two points`; `verified 500/500 and 2,000/2,000`.
